content: {"summary":"The release altered the encoding of session keys in redis‑sessions, making old and new pods unable to read each other’s data. Rolling back caused a second wave of logout because the old version could not decode sessions written by the new version. The documented safe action is to deploy a fix‑forward version that understands both encodings, not to roll back.","likely_cause":"Rollback would re‑expose incompatibility – old pods cannot read sessions written by the new version, leading to additional user logouts.","confidence":"high","claims":[{"text":"The release changed how session values under the `sess:` prefix were encoded, causing incompatibility between pod versions.","evidence_ids":["RB-026#4"],"quote":"A release changed how session values under the `sess:` prefix in redis-sessions were encoded."},{"text":"Rolling back triggered a second logout wave because old pods couldn’t read new‑format sessions.","evidence_ids":["RB-026#4"],"quote":"From 14:23, as the first old-version pod returned, everyone who had logged in since 14:08 was logged out a second time"},{"text":"A later version was shipped that reads both encodings, avoiding the need to roll back.","evidence_ids":["RB-026#4"],"quote":"On 2026-07-22 we shipped a version that reads both encodings"},{"text":"The runbook’s Q5 recommendation was to fix‑forward rather than roll back.","evidence_ids":["RB-026#4"],"quote":"Looking back, the answer at Q5 was fix-forward"}],"next_checks":["Confirm the currently deployed auth-service version can read both old and new session encodings","Monitor AUTH‑E401X error rate after any rollback attempt","Verify no new session writes are occurring in the incompatible format","Check that the fix‑forward deployment (reads both formats) is fully rolled out and stable"]}
